rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 4-5 (Tables 1-6, Figs 4-7) report the authors' own proof-of-concept implementation of a flow-sensor (YF-201) IoT device signing Ethereum transactions over LoRaWAN, benchmarked on six microcontroller boards for program size, memory, processing time, energy (Otii meter), and Ropsten transaction cost/time.
rows.notes: The study does not report any result of its own on trust, data sharing among farmers, or coordination of water use. Trustworthiness of the sensed data is asserted by architectural design (device-signed transactions, Section 3), not measured; no farmers, stakeholders or water-sharing outcomes were studied. What the study shows is technical feasibility and overhead (about 6% extra energy, 45% payload compression, ~32 s average transaction processing time) of constrained metering devices acting directly on a public blockchain, which is a precondition for the claimed social effect.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 4-5 (Tables 1-6, Figs 4-7) report the authors' own proof-of-concept and benchmarking experiments on six IoT boards and the Ropsten Ethereum testnet.
rows.notes: No water-use, water-savings or water-use-efficiency outcome is measured. The rewarding smart contract (Reward(cx) relative to a usage threshold, Section 4.3) is only implemented and its gas cost reported (Table 5); no irrigation or water consumption data from farmers are collected, and the irrigation schedule in Section 5.5 is an assumed scenario for the energy-budget model. The study supports only the technical feasibility of the metering-plus-blockchain architecture, a precondition of the claimed efficiency effect.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is an engineering proof-of-concept and benchmark (energy, memory, processing time, blockchain transaction cost/latency); it contains no field or social evaluation of water management outcomes, so neither claimed effect (trust/sharing among farmers; water-use efficiency) is supported by the study's own results.
